NOVELTY: Unlike prior federated meta-learning and variance-reduction methods, Meta-FL explicitly leverages client-side meta-learning to adapt local models before aggregation, formally characterized under a defined heterogeneity model with theoretical insights on convergence improvements. It uniquely combines rigorous empirical validation under extreme non-IID scenarios with practical overhead assessments on edge devices, providing a comprehensive evaluation of meta-learning’s benefits over established variance-reduction baselines like SCAFFOLD.

topic: Federated learning with heterogeneous and non-IID data
text:
IDEA:  
Adaptive personalized aggregation weights that dynamically incorporate client data heterogeneity and size reduce federated learning global training time by at least 20% relative to uniform weighting under realistic non-IID settings.

BACKGROUND:  
Federated learning on heterogeneous, non-IID client data suffers from client-drift and slow convergence, especially when aggregating local updates with uniform or static weights. Existing methods like FedAvg and SCAFFOLD mitigate drift but do not adapt aggregation weights dynamically based on client data distribution heterogeneity, limiting convergence speed and stability in practical deployments with diverse data and device characteristics.

APPROACH:  
We introduce an adaptive weighting scheme where each client’s aggregation weight at every training round is computed as a function of its local data size and a dynamically updated heterogeneity score measuring the statistical distance (e.g., KL divergence) between its local label distribution and a server-estimated global distribution. A tunable parameter \(\alpha\) controls the influence of heterogeneity, penalizing clients with highly skewed or atypical data to stabilize aggregation and reduce client-drift, while preserving contributions from representative clients. We extend the heterogeneity metric to incorporate feature distribution shifts and update variance to better capture client drift and enable robust weighting.

EXPERIMENT:  
We evaluate on the LEAF benchmark datasets FEMNIST (image classification) and Sentiment140 (text sentiment analysis), simulating 100 clients with realistic non-IID data heterogeneity and computational/network latency profiles. Baselines include FedAvg (uniform size-based weights), SCAFFOLD (variance reduction with uniform weights), and a heuristic static heterogeneity-weighted FedAvg variant. The primary metric is total wall-clock time to reach predefined accuracy thresholds (85% test accuracy for FEMNIST, 0.75 F1 for Sentiment140), measured with realistic timing simulation of communication and client compute heterogeneity. Multiple seeds and convergence stability (accuracy variance) are reported to ensure robustness. The hypothesis is falsified if adaptive weighting does not reduce training time by ≥20% compared to FedAvg or degrades final accuracy.

NOVELTY:  
Unlike prior federated learning approaches that use either uniform or static aggregation weights, our method dynamically adapts aggregation weights every round using a theoretically motivated heterogeneity measure that accounts for both label and feature distribution shifts as well as update variance, with convergence guarantees influenced by the heterogeneity parameter \(\alpha\). This fine-grained, adaptive weighting strategy explicitly targets client-drift reduction and convergence acceleration in realistic heterogeneous environments, advancing beyond control variate methods like SCAFFOLD and static weighting heuristics.

topic: Protein structure prediction beyond AlphaFold
text:
IDEA:  
Integrate experimentally derived conformational ensemble restraints from NMR and SAXS data directly into AlphaFold’s structure prediction pipeline to generate biologically relevant dynamic ensembles that improve modeling of intrinsically disordered regions (IDRs) beyond static predictions.

BACKGROUND:  
While AlphaFold2 achieves high accuracy for folded protein domains, it produces static models with low-confidence predictions in IDRs and does not capture their intrinsic conformational heterogeneity. Existing disorder predictors estimate disorder propensities but lack structural ensemble resolution, and experimental ensemble modeling tools (e.g., ENSEMBLE, ASTEROIDS) rely solely on biophysical data without leveraging deep learning. A critical open problem is bridging AlphaFold’s deep learning framework with experimental ensemble data to model IDRs’ dynamic nature accurately.

APPROACH:  
We propose a hybrid method that incorporates NMR-derived restraints (chemical shift-based secondary structure propensities and NOE distance restraints encoded as additional edge features) and SAXS-derived constraints (radius of gyration and pairwise distance distribution P(r) incorporated as differentiable loss terms) into AlphaFold’s architecture during model optimization, enabling generation of conformational ensembles rather than single static structures. This will involve minimal architectural modification combined with fine-tuning or transfer learning to respect AlphaFold’s inductive biases while effectively leveraging experimental ensemble data.

EXPERIMENT:  
Using a curated set of ~50 proteins with annotated IDRs from DisProt, and available high-quality NMR data from BMRB and SAXS profiles from SASBDB, we will compare ensembles generated by (1) standard AlphaFold2, (2) disorder-specific predictors (SPOT-Disorder2, AlphaFold-Multimer ensembles), and (3) the integrated NMR/SAXS-constrained AlphaFold method. Evaluation metrics include ensemble RMSD (eRMSD) to experimentally derived NMR ensembles, Pearson correlation coefficients >0.8 with SAXS-derived radius of gyration and P(r) functions, and agreement with secondary structure propensities (SSP scores). Statistical significance and robustness will be assessed via bootstrapping and cross-validation; failure to achieve ≥10% improvement in eRMSD or significant correlation gains falsifies the hypothesis.

NOVELTY:  
This approach is the first to directly embed experimentally validated dynamic ensemble restraints into AlphaFold’s deep learning prediction pipeline, addressing the fundamental limitation of static IDR modeling and surpassing prior work by combining physics-based ensemble data with state-of-the-art AI predictions. It bridges the gap between data-driven protein structure prediction and experimental ensemble characterization to provide biologically meaningful conformational ensembles for intrinsically disordered proteins.

topic: Protein structure prediction beyond AlphaFold
text:
IDEA: Integrate dynamic conformational ensemble data from molecular dynamics simulations as probabilistic contact features into AlphaFold’s Evoformer module to improve prediction of functionally relevant protein conformations beyond static structure predictions.

BACKGROUND: While AlphaFold2 achieves near-experimental accuracy for static protein structures, it does not explicitly model protein dynamics or multiple functional conformations critical to biological activity. Existing structure prediction methods largely focus on single static snapshots, limiting insight into conformational ensembles underlying protein function and regulation.

APPROACH: We will extract residue-residue distance distributions and dynamic contact maps from experimentally validated MD trajectories in the Dynameomics database and encode these as probabilistic contact feature matrices integrated into AlphaFold’s input pipeline, replacing or augmenting MSA-derived contacts. The AlphaFold architecture will be fine-tuned on a training subset to output structural ensembles rather than single conformations, optimizing ensemble RMSD and contact map accuracy. Rigorous controls including scrambled contacts, raw MD ensembles, and multiple static predictions will validate specificity.

EXPERIMENT: Performance will be evaluated on proteins with known functionally relevant conformational changes (e.g., adenylate kinase, calmodulin, regulatory kinases) by comparing ensemble RMSD and contact map precision/recall against experimental MD ensembles and independent NMR and cryo-EM ensemble data, benchmarking against baseline AlphaFold2, RoseTTAFold, and ensemble-aware methods. Success requires ≥20% improvement in ensemble RMSD and ≥15% in contact map metrics without loss of static structure accuracy (GDT-TS >85).

NOVELTY: This approach pioneers the direct integration of experimentally validated dynamic ensemble data into AlphaFold’s deep learning framework to predict protein conformational landscapes, advancing beyond prior static or sequence-only methods and enabling functionally relevant ensemble predictions with rigorous experimental validation and controls.

topic: Protein structure prediction beyond AlphaFold
text:
IDEA: Integrate dynamic conformational ensemble features extracted from molecular dynamics simulations into AlphaFold2’s neural network inputs and fine-tune the model to improve prediction accuracy of intrinsically disordered regions compared to AlphaFold2 alone.

BACKGROUND: Although AlphaFold2 achieves near-experimental accuracy on folded protein domains, it struggles to accurately model intrinsically disordered regions (IDRs), which lack stable structures and exhibit conformational heterogeneity. Current sequence-based disorder predictors and AlphaFold’s confidence scores provide limited insight into the dynamic nature of IDRs, highlighting the need for methods that incorporate protein flexibility and ensemble behavior.

APPROACH: We will generate all-atom molecular dynamics (MD) simulations (≥500 ns) for target proteins to extract residue-level dynamic features such as RMSF, secondary structure propensities, and contact frequency maps. These features will be encoded as additional input channels appended to AlphaFold2’s multiple sequence alignments or positional embeddings. The AlphaFold2 network will be fine-tuned using a multi-task objective that jointly optimizes 3D structure prediction and residue-level disorder classification, thereby biasing the model toward incorporating dynamic ensemble information.

EXPERIMENT: Using the DisProt 9.0 database for experimentally validated IDRs, the MDFF benchmark for proteins with known conformational ensembles, and NMR ensemble data from PDB/BMRB as independent test sets, we will compare the enhanced model’s disorder classification AUROC, per-residue RMSD in ordered regions, and correlation (Pearson’s r) between predicted and experimental RMSFs against standard AlphaFold2, AlphaFold-Multimer, and state-of-the-art disorder predictors (IUPred3, SPOT-Disorder2). Ablation studies with randomized MD inputs and statistical significance testing (p < 0.05) on multiple cross-validation folds will validate improvements and control for overfitting.

NOVELTY: This work pioneers the direct integration of physically derived dynamic ensemble features from MD simulations into AlphaFold2’s architecture, moving beyond static structure prediction to model IDR flexibility. Unlike prior approaches relying solely on sequence or static structural data, our method incorporates orthogonal, high-resolution dynamic information to address a fundamental limitation of current deep learning-based protein structure predictors.

topic: Protein structure prediction beyond AlphaFold
text:
IDEA: Integrating enhanced sampling molecular dynamics simulations with AlphaFold2-generated static protein structures improves the accuracy of predicted conformational ensembles under physiological conditions, as validated by superior correlation to experimental NMR relaxation data.

BACKGROUND: While AlphaFold2 provides highly accurate static protein structures, it does not capture conformational dynamics essential for understanding protein function in solution. Existing methods that generate ensembles from experimental NMR data or run MD simulations from experimental structures often fail to leverage the complementary strengths of AlphaFold predictions and dynamic sampling, leaving a gap in accurate modeling of physiologically relevant protein flexibility.

APPROACH: We propose starting from AlphaFold2-predicted structures followed by extensive all-atom MD simulations employing enhanced sampling techniques (e.g., accelerated MD, metadynamics) with rigorously benchmarked force fields (CHARMM36m) to generate dynamic ensembles. These ensembles will be quantitatively evaluated against experimental NMR relaxation datasets by computing predicted order parameters (S^2) using tools like TENSOR2 or Relax, enabling direct residue-level comparison.

EXPERIMENT: Using proteins with both MD trajectories available from the Dynameomics database and corresponding NMR relaxation data from the BMRB, we will compare three ensemble generation approaches— AlphaFold2 + enhanced MD, MD starting from experimentally determined structures, and ensemble methods solely based on experimental data (ENSEMBLE/ASTEROIDS)—via Pearson correlation coefficients of predicted vs. experimental S^2 values. Statistical significance of improvements will be assessed by paired tests, with a ≥0.1 increase in correlation over AlphaFold2 alone defined as success.

NOVELTY: This work uniquely combines state-of-the-art AlphaFold2 static predictions with validated, enhanced-sampling MD protocols and rigorous benchmarking against experimental NMR dynamics data, explicitly addressing prior limitations of short MD timescales and insufficient validation. Unlike previous studies, it systematically quantifies the added value of integrating AlphaFold structures and dynamic simulations in predicting physiologically relevant protein conformational ensembles.

topic: Protein structure prediction beyond AlphaFold
text:
IDEA: Integrate molecular dynamics-derived conformational ensemble features as explicit inputs into deep learning models to improve prediction accuracy of flexible and intrinsically disordered protein regions beyond AlphaFold’s static structure predictions.

BACKGROUND: AlphaFold2 and related models excel in predicting static, well-folded protein structures but struggle to capture the conformational heterogeneity and flexibility inherent in intrinsically disordered regions (IDRs) and flexible protein segments. Current disorder predictors and AlphaFold’s single-structure outputs do not fully reflect dynamic ensembles observed experimentally, limiting our understanding of IDR behavior and function.

APPROACH: We will augment a transformer-based protein structure prediction architecture (e.g., AlphaFold’s open-source framework) by embedding residue-wise dynamic features—such as RMSF, principal components of backbone motions, and contact variability matrices—derived from enhanced sampling molecular dynamics simulations (from PED3 and Dynameomics datasets) alongside sequence and MSA inputs. The model will utilize a multi-modal attention mechanism to jointly learn from static sequence evolution and dynamic conformational ensemble information, aiming to better represent flexible and disordered regions.

EXPERIMENT: We will benchmark on experimentally validated NMR-derived ensembles from the Protein Ensemble Database (PED3) and the DisProt database’s annotated intrinsically disordered regions, comparing our model against AlphaFold2, AlphaFold-Multimer, and SPOT-Disorder2. Success criteria include at least a 10% statistically significant reduction in ensemble RMSD relative to AlphaFold2’s predictions and achieving >0.7 Pearson correlation with experimental residue-specific order parameters (S2) and chemical shift variations; ablation studies will isolate the impact of dynamic features.

NOVELTY: Unlike prior work focused on static structure prediction or sequence-based disorder identification, this approach explicitly incorporates experimentally grounded dynamic ensemble data into deep learning models via advanced multi-modal architectures, providing non-redundant, predictive information beyond sequence and evolutionary signals and thus enabling improved modeling of protein flexibility and disorder.

topic: Quantum advantage in machine learning tasks
text:
IDEA:  
Quantum machine learning models implemented as parameterized quantum circuit classifiers (PQCC) on noisy intermediate-scale quantum (NISQ) devices will demonstrate statistically significant lower sample complexity than classical models for high-dimensional, structured image classification tasks under controlled noise and feature constraints.

BACKGROUND:  
Current quantum machine learning research lacks rigorous empirical validation of quantum advantage in realistic NISQ settings, particularly concerning sample efficiency on challenging, structured, high-dimensional data. Existing studies often do not control for noise effects or align classical and quantum input feature spaces, making it unclear when and if quantum models reduce training data requirements compared to classical baselines. This work addresses the open problem of quantifying sample complexity advantage under practical noise models and comparable data representations.

APPROACH:  
We design PQCCs with explicitly specified hardware-efficient ansätze, limited to 8–12 qubits and circuit depths ≤ 20 layers, trained on noisy quantum simulators calibrated with realistic depolarizing and readout error parameters based on current superconducting qubit devices. Input features for both quantum and classical models are identically preprocessed using PCA or convolutional autoencoders to reduce Fashion-MNIST and CIFAR-10 images to a 16–64 dimensional feature space. Classical baselines include fully connected neural networks and SVMs with RBF kernels, matched in parameter count and trained with optimized hyperparameters. Sample complexity is empirically measured as the minimum training samples needed to reach predefined accuracy thresholds (85% for Fashion-MNIST, 70% for CIFAR-10) across 10-fold cross-validation splits.

EXPERIMENT:  
We conduct controlled, incremental training with progressively larger sample subsets (100 to 10,000 examples), evaluating accuracy and learning curves on both datasets under matched features and model complexities. Statistical significance of sample complexity differences between PQCC and classical baselines is tested via paired t-tests (p < 0.05). Ablation studies modulate noise levels to isolate its impact on PQCC performance and convergence.

NOVELTY:  
This study provides the first rigorously controlled empirical investigation of quantum advantage in sample complexity on realistic, moderately high-dimensional image classification tasks, explicitly accounting for noise and feature parity across models. By integrating detailed noise modeling, fixed feature preprocessing, and matched classical baselines, it advances beyond prior exploratory demonstrations and theoretical bounds, offering a concrete falsification framework for quantum sample efficiency advantage on NISQ devices.

topic: Quantum advantage in machine learning tasks
text:
IDEA:  
Quantum machine learning models trained on data distributions that are classically hard to sample from achieve statistically significant lower generalization error than state-of-the-art classical models, given equal training set sizes, as measured by out-of-sample prediction accuracy on both synthetic quantum and quantum-embedded real-world benchmark tasks.

BACKGROUND:  
Demonstrating a quantum advantage in learning generalization—beyond computational speedups—remains an open challenge, particularly for data distributions exhibiting classical sampling hardness. While prior work has explored quantum models for generative or classification tasks, rigorous connections between classical sampling hardness of data, learnability, and generalization performance are underdeveloped. Establishing whether quantum models can leverage classically intractable data distributions to reduce generalization error would represent a fundamental advance in quantum machine learning theory and practice.

APPROACH:  
We propose to rigorously test the hypothesis that quantum models, specifically parameterized quantum circuits (PQCs) and quantum kernel methods with provably expressive quantum feature maps, outperform classical kernel methods and deep learning architectures on data derived from the Quantum Data Distribution Benchmark (QDD-Bench)—a synthetic dataset constructed from output distributions of random quantum circuits with known classical hardness—and CIFAR-10 images embedded via designed quantum feature maps. Our approach includes theoretically grounding the link between classical sampling hardness and classical generalization limits, incorporating classical approximate samplers as baselines to validate hardness assumptions, and employing comprehensive noise mitigation and optimization strategies to ensure fair training comparisons across quantum and classical models.

EXPERIMENT:  
We evaluate all models on fixed-size training sets with cross-validated hyperparameter tuning, measuring out-of-sample accuracy and generalization error on held-out test sets for QDD-Bench and quantum-embedded CIFAR-10 datasets. Success is defined as at least a 5% absolute reduction in test error by quantum models over the best classical baseline on QDD-Bench, and a 2-3% improvement on CIFAR-10 embeddings, with statistical significance confirmed over multiple independent training runs and confidence intervals. Ablation studies across datasets varying in classical hardness and analyses incorporating classical approximate sampling heuristics will control for data complexity and model capacity factors.

NOVELTY:  
This work advances beyond existing quantum machine learning studies by explicitly linking classical sampling hardness to learnability and generalization gains, rigorously benchmarking against robust classical approximate samplers, and addressing practical quantum training challenges such as noise and barren plateaus with statistical rigor. Unlike prior demonstrations focused on generative modeling or heuristic performance, our study provides a concrete, falsifiable hypothesis about quantum advantage in generalization error grounded on theoretically motivated, classically intractable data distributions.

topic: Quantum advantage in machine learning tasks
text:
IDEA:  
Quantum machine learning models leveraging quantum-native data encodings and problem structure demonstrate superior generalization performance over classical models on tailored quantum-structured learning tasks under rigorously matched resource constraints.

BACKGROUND:  
Current demonstrations of quantum advantage in machine learning using high-dimensional classical datasets like MNIST-C or HIGGS are limited by quantum hardware capabilities and lack clear theoretical justification for advantage. Open problems remain in identifying realistic learning tasks and datasets where quantum models exploit inherent quantum structure to outperform classical counterparts, particularly under fair and measurable resource comparisons.

APPROACH:  
We propose to design and train parameterized quantum models on datasets that embed quantum-native features or symmetries (e.g., quantum chemistry datasets, graph-structured data with quantum-inspired kernels, or synthetic datasets with provable quantum query complexity gaps) using efficient quantum encoding schemes. Classical models employing state-of-the-art architectures and hyperparameter tuning will be trained under matched computational resource budgets defined by wall-clock time, energy consumption estimates, and model expressivity metrics to ensure fairness.

EXPERIMENT:  
Evaluate generalization performance using metrics such as accuracy, AUC, or F1-score on benchmark quantum-structured datasets, while performing systematic ablations over noise levels and error mitigation techniques; quantum and classical training runs will be repeated ≥10 times to assess statistical significance, with the hypothesis falsified if classical models match or exceed quantum model performance at equal or lower resource use across all tasks.

NOVELTY:  
This work distinguishes itself by focusing on learning tasks with intrinsic quantum structure where theoretical arguments suggest quantum advantage, implementing rigorous and quantifiable resource-based comparisons, and conducting comprehensive noise and control studies—moving beyond prior efforts that rely on large classical datasets or hardware-limited heuristics without fair benchmarking frameworks.

topic: Quantum advantage in machine learning tasks
text:
IDEA:  
Quantum machine learning models trained on high-dimensional classical datasets embedding intrinsic quantum correlations achieve a statistically significant lower generalization error than any classical model trained on the same data, demonstrating a fundamental quantum advantage in learning tasks rooted in quantum-correlated features.

BACKGROUND:  
A key open problem in quantum machine learning (QML) is whether intrinsic quantum correlations encoded in classical data confer a provable and practical generalization advantage over classical learning models. Existing studies have explored quantum models on synthetic or small-scale problems but lack rigorous theoretical foundations and comprehensive empirical validation on datasets explicitly constructed to embed quantum correlations. Addressing this gap is critical for substantiating claims of quantum advantage beyond computational complexity arguments.

APPROACH:  
We develop a theoretically justified framework linking quantum correlations in classical datasets to improved learnability by QML, explicitly addressing model expressivity, training dynamics, and mitigating barren plateau effects. Leveraging parameterized quantum circuits (PQCs) with advanced encoding strategies (e.g., amplitude encoding and problem-inspired feature maps), we train QML models on the Quantum Synthetic Dataset (QSD) and Quantum Chemistry Dataset (QChem), both high-dimensional and embedding verified quantum correlations. Classical baselines include optimized deep neural networks (DNNs), Gaussian Process Regression with tailored kernels, and support vector machines (SVMs) with radial basis function kernels, alongside ablation controls on correlation-ablated datasets and classical models incorporating quantum-inspired features.

EXPERIMENT:  
We conduct extensive k-fold cross-validation (k≥10) to measure generalization error via mean squared error (MSE) or classification error on unseen test data, applying rigorous statistical analyses including paired t-tests with multiple hypothesis correction and effect size computation. Success is defined as QML models achieving at least a 10% relative reduction in average generalization error compared to all classical baselines with p < 0.01 significance; failure to do so falsifies the hypothesis. Resource-aware training protocols and dimensionality reduction methods ensure scalability and experimental feasibility on near-term quantum hardware or simulators.

NOVELTY:  
This work rigorously bridges theory and practice by (1) providing explicit complexity-theoretic and learning-theoretic arguments for the source of QML advantage tied to quantum correlations in classical data, (2) experimentally validating this on benchmark datasets with built-in quantum structure using comprehensive classical controls that isolate the role of quantum correlations, and (3) establishing statistically robust, scalable evaluation protocols that surpass prior work limited to toy datasets or heuristic comparisons, thus offering a concrete pathway to verify true quantum advantage in machine learning.

topic: Quantum advantage in machine learning tasks
text:
IDEA:  
Quantum machine learning models demonstrate a provable generalization advantage over classical models exclusively when trained on datasets with rigorously quantified exponentially large latent dimensionality relative to input size, and this advantage can be empirically falsified by classical models matching or surpassing QML performance on such datasets.

BACKGROUND:  
Despite theoretical proposals suggesting quantum advantage in machine learning arises from data distributions with exponentially large latent dimensionality, there is no consensus on how to precisely define or measure latent dimension operationally, nor robust empirical validation isolating its causal role. Existing works often rely on heuristic or qualitative arguments about quantum feature spaces without tightly controlled experimental comparisons against optimally tuned classical baselines on datasets with certified latent complexity.

APPROACH:  
We develop an operational framework to rigorously quantify latent dimensionality via spectral metrics (e.g., effective rank, participation ratio) of data covariance and kernel integral operators, enabling construction and certification of synthetic and real datasets with controllable latent dimension scaling. We benchmark parameterized quantum circuits and quantum kernel methods against enhanced classical baselines—including deep neural networks with quantum-inspired architectures, classical kernels with optimized expressivity, and advanced random feature expansions—under matched computational budgets and systematic hyperparameter tuning to fairly assess generalization performance.

EXPERIMENT:  
We conduct controlled experiments on (1) a quantum-inspired synthetic dataset generated from high-dimensional quantum state simulations with certified exponential latent dimension, (2) MNIST digits embedded via random projections varying latent feature complexity, and (3) the QM9 molecular dataset exhibiting complex quantum-correlated structures. Generalization error, sample complexity, and noise robustness are measured over multiple data splits and random seeds, with quantum advantage defined as a statistically significant (>5% absolute) reduction in generalization error of QML models compared to all classical baselines on datasets with certified exponential latent dimensionality. Failure of QML to outperform classical models under these conditions falsifies the hypothesis.

NOVELTY:  
This work uniquely formalizes latent dimensionality with operationally verifiable metrics and integrates rigorous dataset construction with rigorously optimized classical baselines, enabling a definitive empirical test of the theoretical conjecture linking quantum advantage to latent dimension scaling—going beyond prior qualitative or asymptotic analyses to provide actionable complexity-theoretic insights validated through systematic experimentation.

topic: Causal discovery from observational data
text:
IDEA: Incorporating domain-specific causal constraints as differentiable soft priors into deep learning causal discovery models improves the accuracy and robustness of causal graph recovery from high-dimensional nonlinear time series compared to approaches without such priors.

BACKGROUND: Causal discovery from observational time series data remains challenging due to high dimensionality, nonlinear interactions, and limited sample sizes, especially when ground-truth causal structures are unavailable or uncertain. Existing deep learning frameworks like TCDF demonstrate promising performance but often ignore domain knowledge that could guide and constrain causal inference, limiting identifiability and interpretability.

APPROACH: We extend the Temporal Causal Discovery Framework (TCDF) by integrating domain-informed causal constraints as soft, differentiable regularization terms on the learned adjacency matrices, allowing probabilistic encouragement of plausible causal directions without hard exclusions. These priors are carefully formulated and weighted based on validated physiological knowledge for the PhysioNet Challenge 2012 dataset and physical climate mechanisms for the CMIP6 Climatic Network dataset, with hyperparameters tuned via cross-validation to balance prior influence and data fit.

EXPERIMENT: We evaluate our model on (1) the PhysioNet Challenge 2012 physiological time series with expert-validated causal relationships, (2) the CMIP6 Climatic Network dataset with climate science–based causal annotations, and (3) synthetic nonlinear time series with fully known ground-truth graphs for benchmarking. Performance is measured by precision, recall, and F1-score of recovered causal edges against ground truth, comparing (a) TCDF with soft priors, (b) vanilla TCDF, (c) PCMCI+, and (d) nonlinear conditional independence tests without priors. Rigorous controls include ablation studies with random or incorrect priors and statistical significance testing (Wilcoxon signed-rank test, p < 0.05) to formally falsify the hypothesis if improvements are absent or negative.

NOVELTY: Unlike prior work that applies deep learning or conditional independence testing without principled incorporation of domain knowledge, our method offers a novel, generalizable framework to encode soft causal constraints as differentiable priors, improving identifiability and interpretability in high-dimensional nonlinear time series causal discovery while explicitly addressing the impact and tuning of these priors.

topic: Causal discovery from observational data
text:
IDEA: Incorporate a variational autoencoder-based latent variable model into nonlinear temporal causal discovery frameworks to explicitly model unmeasured confounders, thereby significantly reducing false positive causal links in high-dimensional nonlinear time series data.

BACKGROUND: Existing nonlinear causal discovery methods for high-dimensional time series, such as TCDF and PCMCI+, typically assume causal sufficiency and do not explicitly model latent confounders, leading to elevated false positive rates in inferred causal graphs. Identifying causal relationships in complex dynamical systems with hidden confounding remains an open problem, especially when only observational data are available and confounder effects are nonlinear and high-dimensional.

APPROACH: We extend the Temporal Causal Discovery Framework (TCDF) by jointly optimizing causal adjacency matrices along with a variational autoencoder (VAE) that learns latent confounder embeddings capturing unmeasured influences. Conditional independence tests and causal edge inference are conditioned on these learned latent variables to isolate true causal effects from confounding. Ablation studies will compare this joint VAE approach against simpler latent representations (e.g., PCA) and variants without joint optimization to isolate the impact of our latent confounder modeling.

EXPERIMENT: We evaluate on the Lorenz 96 multivariate chaotic system with known ground truth causal structure and controllable latent confounders, and on Human Connectome Project (HCP) fMRI time series data leveraging partial neuroscientific ground truth and stability-based evaluation metrics. Metrics include false positive rate (FPR), structural Hamming distance (SHD), and statistical significance tests (paired Wilcoxon) over multiple random seeds and varying latent confounder complexities. Baselines are TCDF, PCMCI+, and CAnDOIT (which uses interventional data but no latent modeling). Success is defined as at least a 20% reduction in FPR and SHD compared to the best baseline; failure to reduce these metrics by at least 5% falsifies the hypothesis.

NOVELTY: Unlike prior nonlinear causal discovery methods that assume causal sufficiency or rely on interventional data, our method explicitly models nonlinear latent confounders within a deep generative framework jointly optimized with causal structure learning, accompanied by rigorous ablation analyses and theoretical identifiability discussions to substantiate the foundational validity and isolate the contributions of latent confounder modeling.

topic: Causal discovery from observational data
text:
IDEA: Incorporating rigorously constructed domain-specific causal edge constraints as probabilistic priors into nonlinear causal discovery algorithms for high-dimensional observational time series significantly reduces false positive causal edges without compromising recall.

BACKGROUND: Causal discovery from high-dimensional, nonlinear observational time series remains challenged by spurious edges due to limited sample sizes and complex dependencies. While domain knowledge can theoretically guide causal inference, existing methods rarely quantify or validate the benefit of integrating expert-derived causal constraints, especially in nonlinear deep learning frameworks. This gap complicates reliable causal graph recovery in critical domains like neuroscience and climate science where partial but uncertain prior knowledge exists.

APPROACH: We augment the Temporal Causal Discovery Framework (TCDF) by encoding domain constraints as a probabilistic mask over possible causal edges, using Bayesian regularization to softly encourage edges supported by expert knowledge and exclude implausible connections. This approach balances constraint-driven guidance with data-driven discovery, allowing for uncertainty and partial knowledge. Sensitivity analyses with randomized and misspecified constraints assess robustness, while additional validation on synthetic datasets with known ground truth ensures interpretability.

EXPERIMENT: We evaluate the constrained TCDF alongside baselines PCMCI+ and unconstrained TCDF on high-dimensional fMRI data from the Human Connectome Project and NOAA climate time series, measuring Structural Hamming Distance, precision, recall, and false positive rate against literature-validated causal edges and interventional subsets. Statistical significance is tested via paired bootstrap tests over repeated runs, with falsification defined by failure to reduce false positives by ≥20% without >10% F1 score degradation.

NOVELTY: Unlike prior work that applies hard domain constraints or purely data-driven methods, our approach introduces a theoretically justified, flexible Bayesian integration of domain knowledge into nonlinear causal discovery, explicitly addressing constraint uncertainty and scalability in complex real-world time series. This enables principled mitigation of false positives while preserving discovery power, supported by rigorous robustness controls and sensitivity analyses not previously conducted.

topic: Causal discovery from observational data
text:
IDEA: Incorporating rigorously validated domain-specific symbolic constraints as priors within nonlinear time series causal discovery algorithms improves the accuracy of recovered causal graphs compared to purely data-driven methods, as demonstrated by statistically significant gains in precision, recall, and F1-score on synthetic and real-world benchmarks with known or partially validated ground-truth.

BACKGROUND: Causal discovery from nonlinear observational time series is challenging due to complex interactions, noise, and limited samples, often resulting in uncertain causal graphs. While recent methods rely primarily on data-driven conditional independence tests or deep learning approaches, effectively integrating domain knowledge to guide causal inference remains an open problem, particularly in nonlinear dynamical systems where mechanistic understanding can provide valuable constraints.

APPROACH: We propose augmenting state-of-the-art nonlinear time series causal discovery algorithms (e.g., PCMCI+ and TCDF) with domain-specific symbolic constraints—such as known mechanistic relations, temporal precedence, and invariant system properties—encoded as hard or soft priors within the graph search scoring functions. This integration explicitly penalizes causal graphs violating domain constraints while preserving model flexibility, and includes systematic validation and tuning of constraints to mitigate bias and ensure robustness.

EXPERIMENT: We will evaluate performance on the Lorenz-96 and Friedman nonlinear time series benchmarks, alongside the Human Activity Recognition Using Smartphones (HAR) dataset with partially validated causal links, measuring precision, recall, F1-score, and false positive rate over multiple noise and sample size conditions. Statistical significance of at least a 10% absolute F1-score improvement over unconstrained PCMCI+ and TCDF baselines will validate the hypothesis, while cross-validation and sensitivity analyses will control for overfitting and constraint misspecification.

NOVELTY: Unlike prior work relying solely on data-driven testing or black-box models, our approach explicitly formalizes symbolic domain knowledge as flexible priors within nonlinear causal discovery frameworks, systematically validating constraint accuracy and robustness. This theoretical and methodological rigor enables principled integration of domain expertise, providing formal guarantees and practical guidelines absent from existing nonlinear causal discovery literature.

topic: Causal discovery from observational data
text:
IDEA:  
Incorporate domain-specific causal constraints as hard or soft priors into the Temporal Causal Discovery Framework (TCDF) to reduce false positive causal links in high-dimensional nonlinear time series, while preserving recall, compared to purely data-driven methods.

BACKGROUND:  
Causal discovery from observational nonlinear time series data is challenging due to high dimensionality, complex dependencies, and limited samples, often resulting in numerous spurious causal edges. Existing unsupervised methods, including TCDF and nonlinear conditional independence-based approaches, rely solely on data and struggle to balance false positives and recall. Leveraging expert domain knowledge to inform causal search is hypothesized to improve precision but lacks rigorous validation, theoretical grounding, and practical evaluation in large-scale nonlinear dynamical systems.

APPROACH:  
We propose extending TCDF by integrating domain-specific causal constraints—such as known causal directions, forbidden edges, and required links—as penalty terms in the loss function and/or search space restrictions during graph optimization. We rigorously model constraint strength and correctness, performing ablation studies with correct, incorrect, and partial constraints to assess robustness. The method will be theoretically justified via a Bayesian prior interpretation and identifiability analysis to explain how domain knowledge guides causal discovery without compromising recall in nonlinear, high-dimensional time series.

EXPERIMENT:  
We will evaluate on synthetic nonlinear dynamical systems (e.g., Lorenz-96) with fully known causal graphs, CMIP5 climate datasets with expert-validated physical causal relationships, and PhysioNet Challenge 2012 physiological time series with expert-annotated causal links. Baselines include vanilla TCDF and the nonlinear conditional independence test method by Runge et al. (2019). Metrics are precision, recall, F1-score, and false positive rate (FPR), with success defined as a statistically significant >20% relative reduction in FPR while maintaining recall above 90% of baseline, assessed via bootstrapped splits and synthetic data realizations.

NOVELTY:  
This work uniquely integrates domain constraints directly into the TCDF deep learning framework via principled priors and constrained optimization, distinguishing it from prior constraint-based or score-based methods that do not leverage deep temporal representations. It systematically quantifies the impact of constraint correctness and strength on causal accuracy and scalability, providing theoretical insights and practical feasibility analyses for scalable, knowledge-informed causal discovery in complex nonlinear time series.

topic: Scaling laws for Large Language Models
text:
IDEA:  
Investigate how the scaling efficiency of large language models (LLMs) trained on mixed-domain corpora degrades non-linearly with increasing semantic divergence between domains, using a model-aligned semantic divergence metric and across multiple model scales.

BACKGROUND:  
While existing scaling laws characterize LLM performance as functions of model size, data volume, and compute, the impact of mixed-domain training data with varying semantic distances remains poorly understood. In particular, it is unclear whether and how increasing semantic divergence between training domains non-linearly impairs scaling efficiency, a critical question for multi-domain pretraining and domain adaptation strategies.

APPROACH:  
We propose to quantify semantic divergence using embedding-based metrics derived directly from intermediate layers of pretrained LLMs to better reflect model-internal representations and learning difficulty. We will pretrain GPT-style decoder-only Transformers at multiple scales (100M, 1B, 10B parameters) on controlled mixtures of a high-quality general corpus (the Pile) combined with domain-specific corpora of increasing semantic divergence—scientific Wikipedia articles (WikiSci), arXiv CS/physics papers, and biomedical texts (PubMed/PMC)—at varied mixture ratios. Scaling efficiency will be measured by cross-entropy loss reduction rates on held-out domain-specific benchmarks, fitted against semantic divergence metrics to detect nonlinear degradation patterns.

EXPERIMENT:  
Train models on mixture ratios (100:0, 90:10, 70:30, 50:50) of general-to-domain data across three domain sets and evaluate on SciQ (WikiSci), arXiv summarization, and BLURB biomedical benchmarks using cross-entropy loss and perplexity. Fit linear and nonlinear models to relate semantic divergence to relative scaling efficiency across model sizes. Baselines include single-domain and pure general corpus training, plus naive linear interpolation of known scaling laws.

NOVELTY:  
This work introduces a model-aligned, dynamically validated semantic divergence metric for analyzing domain interaction effects on LLM scaling efficiency, expands the study across multiple model scales, and rigorously isolates semantic divergence from confounding dataset factors—advancing beyond prior studies focused on fixed architectures, single-scale observations, or simplistic divergence measures.

topic: Scaling laws for Large Language Models
text:
IDEA:  
The optimal scaling behavior of large language models trained on mixed-domain corpora deviates from classical smooth power-law scaling, exhibiting statistically robust piecewise scaling breakpoints whose locations systematically correlate with measured domain divergence intensity.

BACKGROUND:  
While existing scaling laws for LLMs (e.g., Kaplan et al., 2020; “Predictable Scale,” 2025) assume smooth power-law improvements with increasing model size and data, they do not explicitly address how heterogeneous domain mixtures induce fundamental changes in scaling dynamics. Mixed-domain training is widely used in practice but poorly understood theoretically, especially regarding whether domain shifts cause discrete regime changes (“breakpoints”) in loss scaling rather than gradual transitions. Clarifying this is critical to optimize training strategies for multi-domain LLMs and to better predict performance and transferability.

APPROACH:  
We will rigorously quantify domain divergence using embedding-based metrics (e.g., Jensen-Shannon divergence on Sentence-BERT embeddings) and train families of decoder-only transformer LLMs (125M to 1B parameters for feasibility) on carefully curated mixed datasets composed of paired domains with low, medium, and high semantic divergence (e.g., Wikipedia + BookCorpus, Wikipedia + arXiv, Wikipedia + GitHub code). For each mixture ratio (25/75, 50/50, 75/25), we fit both smooth power-law and piecewise power-law scaling models to validation cross-entropy loss curves, applying segmented regression with bootstrapped confidence intervals and multiple hypothesis correction to assess breakpoint robustness.

EXPERIMENT:  
We will measure held-out loss on mixed-domain test sets and individual domain test sets, comparing goodness-of-fit metrics (R², AIC/BIC) between pure and piecewise power-law fits across mixtures. Success requires (a) statistically significant improvement in piecewise model fits for medium and high divergence mixtures (p < 0.01), and (b) breakpoint locations showing positive correlations (Pearson’s r > 0.7) with domain divergence values. Baselines include models trained on pure domains and prior scaling laws assuming smooth scaling. Additionally, we evaluate transfer performance on out-of-distribution benchmarks (GLUE for text, CodeSearchNet for code) to interpret practical impacts of scaling deviations.

NOVELTY:  
Unlike prior work that treats domain mixtures as smooth interpolations of scaling behavior or relies on grid search for mixture ratios (e.g., D-CPT Law, 2024), this study uniquely hypothesizes and empirically validates the existence of discrete scaling regime shifts tied mechanistically to domain divergence. The explicit linkage of breakpoint detection to a theoretically motivated, quantitative domain divergence metric and rigorous statistical validation distinguishes it from prior scaling law analyses that assume monolithic data distributions. This insight can fundamentally reshape data curation and model sizing strategies for multi-domain LLM training.

topic: Scaling laws for Large Language Models
text:
IDEA: Incorporating an adaptive mixture ratio scheduler that dynamically adjusts the proportions of general and domain-specific data during continual pre-training can improve scaling efficiency and domain adaptation in large language models relative to fixed mixture ratios, conditional on measurable domain distinctness and careful tuning.

BACKGROUND: Selecting optimal mixture ratios between general-domain and domain-specific corpora for continual pre-training of LLMs is typically done via costly grid search and often assumes static ratios throughout training. Existing scaling laws and CPT studies do not account for dynamic data mixture adjustments that could better leverage domain informativeness or mitigate overfitting. This leaves open how adaptive data scheduling can systematically improve training efficiency and final performance across distinct domains.

APPROACH: We propose an adaptive mixture ratio scheduler embedded in the continual pre-training loop that updates the data mix every fixed interval (e.g., 10k steps) based on quantitative signals—such as domain validation perplexity plateaus detected via statistical smoothing and divergence measures, domain classifier confidence trends, and overfitting indicators on held-out general data. The scheduler increases domain data proportion when adaptation slows and reverses when overfitting emerges, learning a mixture trajectory without manual grid search. We formalize domain distinctness using distributional divergence (e.g., Jensen-Shannon divergence) between general and domain data embeddings to contextualize expected benefits.

EXPERIMENT: We validate on two markedly distinct domain datasets—MATH (mathematical problem-solving) and PubMed Central Open Access (biomedical)—using SlimPajama as the general corpus. Baselines include fixed-ratio mixtures (100% general, 80/20, 50/50, 20/80, 100% domain) with grid search as per D-CPT Law (2024), naive 100% domain continual pre-training, and random or ablated schedulers. Metrics measure domain validation perplexity reductions (≥3% improvement), compute efficiency gains (≥10% GPU hour savings to reach target perplexities of 12 for MATH and 14 for PMCOA), and robustness across multiple seeds. Compute efficiency is assessed with noise-robust early stopping and smoothing protocols for fair cross-run comparisons.

NOVELTY: Unlike prior work relying on static or manually grid-searched mixture ratios, this research introduces a theoretically grounded, statistically principled adaptive scheduler that leverages domain distinctness signals to improve scaling efficiency in domain-specific continual pre-training, explicitly quantifying when and why adaptive data mixtures outperform fixed baselines across heterogeneous domains and compute budgets.

topic: Scaling laws for Large Language Models
text:
IDEA:  
Investigate how scaling laws of large multimodal language models trained on carefully normalized mixtures of balanced, high-quality text and image datasets follow continuous power-law trends with modality-ratio-dependent deviations explained by representation alignment and data quality metrics.

BACKGROUND:  
Current scaling laws for large language models primarily focus on unimodal text data, leaving open how these laws generalize to multimodal models across varying modality ratios. Realistic multimodal training involves complex interactions between modalities with distinct data characteristics and alignment challenges, making it unclear whether smooth power-law scaling persists or if sharp deviations arise due to modality-specific factors. Resolving this is critical for principled compute allocation and model design in multimodal AI.

APPROACH:  
We propose training a family of transformer-based multimodal models (Vision Transformer encoder + GPT-style decoder with cross-modal attention) across a spectrum of text-to-image ratios, using balanced, large-scale, and quality-controlled datasets—specifically LAION-2B (image-caption pairs) for visual modality and a filtered subset of The Pile for text. We normalize training by effective information content (e.g., bytes or FLOPs) rather than raw token/image counts to ensure comparable compute budgets. Representation alignment is quantitatively measured via embedding similarity metrics, and ablations with noisier datasets (e.g., Conceptual Captions) and architectural variants probe modality-specific effects.

EXPERIMENT:  
Evaluate held-out cross-entropy loss scaling and zero-shot downstream performance (COCO Captioning accuracy and WikiText-103 perplexity) for each modality ratio and model size (100M to 10B parameters). Apply piecewise power-law fitting with breakpoint detection to detect deviations, correlating these with alignment quality and data noise. Baselines include pure text-only and pure vision-language unimodal models trained under matched conditions. Falsification criteria include non-monotonic or discontinuous scaling curves or catastrophic loss jumps upon small modality ratio shifts.

NOVELTY:  
Unlike prior work that either studies single-modality scaling or multimodal pretraining at fixed ratios without rigorous normalization, this work explicitly controls for dataset scale and quality imbalances, introduces principled normalization metrics, and quantitatively links representation alignment to scaling deviations. This provides the first mechanistically grounded and statistically robust characterization of multimodal scaling laws across modality mixtures.

topic: Scaling laws for Large Language Models
text:
IDEA:  
Investigate whether the scaling exponent for loss reduction in large language models differs between general-domain pre-training and domain-specific continual pre-training (CPT), with domain-specific CPT exhibiting significantly smaller scaling exponents—indicating diminishing returns at smaller model sizes—by conducting a rigorously controlled empirical study incorporating adaptive CPT schedules and dataset overlap controls.

BACKGROUND:  
While scaling laws for language models are well-established in general-domain settings, it remains unclear how these laws translate to domain-specific continual pre-training. Prior work such as the D-CPT Law (2024) highlights mixture ratio optimization but does not conclusively characterize how scaling behavior differs by domain or CPT versus training-from-scratch approaches. This gap limits principled guidance on model sizing and compute allocation for domain-adapted LLMs.

APPROACH:  
We pre-train a suite of decoder-only Transformer models (100M to 3B parameters in a pilot phase) on general-domain corpora (SlimPajama + The Pile), then perform CPT on code (CodeParrot) and biomedical (PubMed Central OA) datasets using adaptive mixture ratios and fixed token budgets tailored per model size. Parallel control groups train domain-specific models from scratch on the same datasets. We fit power-law scaling curves \(L(N) = L_0 + kN^{-\alpha}\) to cross-entropy losses on held-out domain-specific test sets, applying statistical tests to compare scaling exponents \(\alpha\) across conditions.

EXPERIMENT:  
Evaluate cross-entropy loss scaling on held-out general, code, and biomedical test sets across model sizes and training regimens, controlling for domain overlap via filtered corpora. Quantify significance of differences in scaling exponents \(\alpha_{CPT}\) vs. \(\alpha_{general}\) and versus domain-specific from-scratch baselines using bootstrap confidence intervals.

NOVELTY:  
This work systematically isolates the impact of domain-specific CPT on fundamental scaling behavior with adaptive training protocols and overlap controls, addressing limitations in prior scaling law studies and the D-CPT Law by providing the first statistically rigorous evidence of domain-dependent scaling exponents—and thereby informs optimal model sizing and compute strategies for domain-specific LLM deployment.

topic: Energy-efficient neuromorphic computing
text:
IDEA: Integrating thermoelectric energy harvesters with low-power neuromorphic processors reduces total system battery energy consumption by over 30% during spiking neural network inference tasks compared to identical processors powered solely by conventional batteries.

BACKGROUND: Energy efficiency remains a critical bottleneck for the deployment of neuromorphic computing systems in real-world, always-on applications. While emerging memristive and quantum-material devices improve device-level efficiency, system-level gains are limited by reliance on conventional battery power and lack of sustainable energy harvesting integration. Thermoelectric energy harvesters (TEHs) offer a promising approach to reclaim ambient thermal gradients, but their practical impact on neuromorphic system energy consumption under realistic workloads is not well quantified.

APPROACH: We propose a controlled integration of commercially available TEHs with a state-of-the-art neuromorphic processor (e.g., Intel Loihi 2), coupled with precise power management circuitry to maximize harvested energy utilization. The system will be evaluated under steady, reproducible thermal gradients in a lab environment, running representative spiking neural network inference tasks on the N-MNIST and DVS Gesture datasets. High-precision instrumentation will separately monitor battery drain, harvested energy contribution, and parasitic losses, enabling accurate measurement of net system energy savings.

EXPERIMENT: The experiment compares total battery energy consumption over 8-hour inference sessions between two setups: (1) Loihi 2 powered solely by lithium-ion battery, and (2) Loihi 2 integrated with TEH and power management, both running identical workloads and operating conditions. Success is defined as achieving more than 30% reduction in battery energy draw with TEH integration, while savings below 15% will falsify the hypothesis. Secondary metrics include inference latency and accuracy to ensure no performance degradation.

NOVELTY: Unlike prior work focusing on device-level neuromorphic innovations or theoretical harvesting potential, this study rigorously quantifies system-level energy efficiency gains from practical TEH integration under real-world spiking workloads. It incorporates a validated theoretical model to set realistic energy-saving targets and transparently accounts for overheads, bridging the gap between laboratory device research and deployable, sustainable neuromorphic systems.

topic: Energy-efficient neuromorphic computing
text:
IDEA:  
Integrating memristive synapses with quantum-dot-based stochastic neurons reduces neuromorphic system energy consumption by at least 30% per inference on the N-MNIST dataset compared to fully memristor-based architectures, while maintaining accuracy within 1%.

BACKGROUND:  
Energy efficiency remains a critical bottleneck in neuromorphic computing hardware, where conventional deterministic neuron circuits often incur significant overhead. Though memristor-based synapses have demonstrated promising low-power synaptic functionalities, deterministic memristor neurons add complexity and energy cost. Leveraging the intrinsic stochasticity of quantum-dot devices as probabilistic neurons offers a novel pathway to reduce neuron circuit energy without sacrificing performance, addressing the challenge of scaling energy-efficient neuromorphic systems.

APPROACH:  
We propose a hybrid neuromorphic architecture combining memristive synapses with quantum-dot stochastic neurons that probabilistically generate spikes via charge trapping/detrapping dynamics, eliminating complex neuron circuitry. Both the hybrid and fully memristor-based baselines are designed with matched device counts, topologies, and operating voltages to isolate energy savings attributable to neuron implementation. Weight programming and spike generation are controlled via voltage pulse schemes validated through device-level modeling and fabrication or high-fidelity emulation with environmental stability measures.

EXPERIMENT:  
Energy per inference, spike counts, latency, and classification accuracy will be measured on two hardware prototypes executing a two-layer spiking neural network with a hidden layer of 256 neurons trained on the N-MNIST benchmark. On-chip power sensors or calibrated external micro-watt resolution measurement equipment will record energy consumption over >30 repeated trials to capture variability. The hypothesis is falsified if the hybrid system fails to achieve ≥30% energy reduction relative to the memristor-only baseline or if accuracy differs by more than 1%.

NOVELTY:  
This work differentiates itself by harnessing the unique physical stochasticity of quantum-dot neurons as inherent probabilistic spiking elements integrated with memristive synapses, enabling neuron energy reduction beyond what prior stochastic neuron models or memristor-based neurons offer. It rigorously quantifies energy savings in a matched hardware setting while validating functional equivalence and elucidating trade-offs in spike dynamics and inference latency.

topic: Energy-efficient neuromorphic computing
text:
IDEA: Integrating phase-change materials (PCMs) with HfO₂-based memristive synapses can reduce total synaptic energy consumption by at least 30% during neuromorphic inference tasks without compromising accuracy, by leveraging PCM-enabled dynamic thresholding and plasticity control.

BACKGROUND: Current memristor-based neuromorphic hardware achieves promising energy efficiency but faces limitations in dynamic plasticity and non-volatile thresholding that increase power consumption during synaptic updates and inference. Existing memristive devices lack robust mechanisms to modulate synaptic dynamics with low energy overhead, hindering scalable, energy-efficient neuromorphic systems. This work targets these challenges by hybridizing memristors with PCMs to enable energy-saving synaptic control while maintaining computational equivalence.

APPROACH: We propose fabricating and benchmarking two comparable neuromorphic arrays: (1) a baseline array of HfO₂ memristors implementing synaptic weights, and (2) a hybrid array integrating PCM elements co-located with memristors to provide non-volatile thresholding and short-term plasticity modulation. Both arrays will run identical spiking neural networks—two-layer Leaky Integrate-and-Fire for MNIST and a convolutional SNN for CIFAR-10—with standardized device programming to align conductance states. Energy consumption, latency, throughput, and accuracy will be measured at the device level using high-resolution on-chip instrumentation and normalized per inference.

EXPERIMENT: The core falsification test compares total synaptic energy per inference across thousands of cycles for both arrays performing MNIST and CIFAR-10 classification, with accuracy maintained within ±1% of the baseline. A ≥30% reduction in energy use by the hybrid system validates the hypothesis; failure to meet this threshold or accuracy degradation falsifies it. Detailed ablation studies will isolate the PCM contribution to energy savings, controlling for peripheral overhead and switching dynamics.

NOVELTY: Unlike previous work focusing solely on memristor devices or PCM phase transitions independently, this study pioneers a rigorously controlled hybrid neuromorphic synapse architecture combining PCMs and HfO₂ memristors, with comprehensive system-level benchmarking and energy modeling. It uniquely quantifies practical energy savings and computational trade-offs at scale, addressing fabrication integration challenges and establishing clear metrics for scalable, energy-efficient neuromorphic hardware design.

topic: Energy-efficient neuromorphic computing
text:
IDEA: Integrating Bi₂Se₃ topological insulator layers into HfO₂-based memristive synapses will reduce switching energy consumption by at least 30% compared to conventional memristors through suppression of electron backscattering at the switching interface, while maintaining ≥97% classification accuracy on MNIST.

BACKGROUND: Conventional HfO₂-based memristors exhibit significant energy loss during switching due to electron backscattering and Joule heating, limiting their energy efficiency in neuromorphic computing. Leveraging topological insulator (TI) surface states to suppress backscattering presents a promising but experimentally unverified route to reduce switching energy in memristive synapses without compromising device reliability or system-level performance.

APPROACH: Fabricate two matched sets of memristive devices—standard HfO₂ memristors and HfO₂ memristors with an integrated Bi₂Se₃ TI interfacial layer—ensuring controlled interface quality via TEM, XPS, and SIMS analyses. Characterize switching energy, retention, endurance, and transient switching dynamics (including temperature mapping), complemented by backscattering proxy measurements using low-temperature magnetotransport and noise spectroscopy. Integrate devices into crossbar arrays and benchmark neuromorphic performance on the MNIST dataset using the NeuroSim simulator extended with custom TI energy models.

EXPERIMENT: Measure the average energy per synaptic weight update over 10,000 SET/RESET cycles and classification accuracy on MNIST; success requires ≥30% energy reduction relative to standard HfO₂ devices and ≥97% accuracy. Validate suppression of electron backscattering through correlated noise and magnetotransport signatures. Failure to demonstrate these improvements or observing accuracy below 95% falsifies the hypothesis.

NOVELTY: This work uniquely combines direct experimental validation of TI-induced backscattering suppression with rigorous interface characterization and system-level neuromorphic benchmarking, advancing beyond prior memristor energy-efficiency studies that lack topological material integration and explicit causal linkage to electron transport phenomena.

topic: Energy-efficient neuromorphic computing
text:
IDEA: Incorporating ferroelectric domain wall motion into memristive synapses reduces energy consumption per synaptic write event by at least 30% compared to conventional HfO₂-based filamentary memristors under identical operating conditions.

BACKGROUND: Energy efficiency is a critical bottleneck in scaling neuromorphic computing hardware, where synaptic devices dominate power budgets. Conventional filamentary memristors, such as ALD-fabricated HfO₂ devices, rely on conductive filament formation and rupture, which incur significant switching energy and variability. Ferroelectric domain wall memristors (FDWMs) offer a fundamentally different resistance switching mechanism that promises lower energy dissipation and improved endurance, but quantitative comparative benchmarks under realistic neuromorphic workloads remain lacking.

APPROACH: We will fabricate two 1T1R memristor synaptic arrays: (1) FDWMs using engineered doped ferroelectric HfO₂ or PZT thin films optimized for domain wall motion switching, and (2) baseline ALD HfO₂ filamentary memristors following established protocols. Both arrays will be integrated on identical hardware testbeds to run inference on the N-MNIST spiking neuromorphic vision dataset, enabling direct energy, speed, and endurance benchmarking under matched pulse schemes calibrated to ensure equivalent synaptic weight modulation.

EXPERIMENT: Using high-precision current-voltage sensing with parasitic-aware calibration, we will measure average energy consumption per synaptic write event, switching latency, and endurance (targeting >10⁶ cycles) for both device types during spiking neural network inference on N-MNIST. Success requires FDWMs to demonstrate ≥30% energy reduction compared to filamentary memristors (e.g., ≤7 pJ vs. 10 pJ per pulse) without >20% switching speed degradation or compromised endurance.

NOVELTY: This work is the first to rigorously quantify the energy-efficiency advantage of ferroelectric domain wall memristors over state-of-the-art filamentary HfO₂ devices within a system-relevant neuromorphic inference context, leveraging calibrated measurement protocols and endurance/speed metrics grounded in domain wall switching theory—thus providing a decisive test of the proposed switching physics for next-generation low-power synapses.

topic: Generative AI for drug discovery and molecular design
text:
IDEA: Integrating multi-omics data (genomics, transcriptomics, metabolomics) with chemical structure information into generative AI models will yield novel drug candidates exhibiting significantly improved in vitro efficacy on relevant cancer cell lines compared to models trained solely on chemical structures.

BACKGROUND: Current generative AI approaches in drug discovery predominantly leverage chemical structure data, limiting their ability to account for complex biological contexts that influence drug efficacy. Incorporating multi-omics profiles from standardized cancer cell lines holds promise for capturing the biological heterogeneity underlying drug response, yet robust methods to integrate and leverage such heterogeneous data in generative models remain lacking. This research addresses the challenge of biologically meaningful data fusion to enhance the predictive power and practical utility of AI-driven molecular design.

APPROACH: We propose a multi-modal generative pipeline that combines latent embeddings of multi-omics datasets—including genomics and transcriptomics from TCGA, metabolomics from the Metabolomics Workbench, and drug sensitivity profiles from GDSC—with molecular latent representations extracted via a Transformer-based variational autoencoder trained on ChEMBL 31 chemical structures. Dimensionality reduction and autoencoder-based embeddings will harmonize heterogeneous omics features, which are concatenated to molecular vectors before molecule generation and optimization via reinforcement learning guided by a bioactivity predictor trained on integrated data. Synthetic accessibility and compound stability assessments will screen candidates prior to synthesis.

EXPERIMENT: We will compare the baseline REINVENT 4 model trained solely on ChEMBL structures against the multi-omics integrated model by synthesizing and testing matched sets of generated molecules on selected cancer cell lines with corresponding omics profiles. Primary metrics include statistically significant reductions (>20%, p<0.05) in mean IC50 values and at least a 15% increase in hit rate (IC50 <1 μM) over baseline, assessed across multiple biological replicates and controlled for synthetic feasibility.

NOVELTY: This work uniquely advances generative AI drug design by rigorously integrating biologically grounded, high-quality multi-omics data with chemical structure representations within a unified generative framework, supported by detailed data mapping strategies and experimental validation. Unlike prior studies that focus on chemical or proteomic data alone, it establishes a validated theoretical and empirical foundation for multi-modal biological context fusion to drive more effective and actionable drug candidate generation.

topic: Generative AI for drug discovery and molecular design
text:
IDEA: Integrating multi-modal biomedical data—including gene expression profiles, protein structural embeddings, and pharmacokinetic parameters—into a conditional variational autoencoder generative model will produce drug candidates with significantly improved in vitro efficacy compared to models trained solely on chemical structure data.

BACKGROUND: Current generative AI approaches in drug discovery predominantly rely on chemical structure data, limiting their ability to capture complex biological contexts that influence drug efficacy. Incorporating heterogeneous biomedical modalities can enrich latent molecular representations, potentially enabling generation of candidates better tailored to biological mechanisms and pharmacological behavior, an open challenge due to data heterogeneity and integration complexity.

APPROACH: We propose a multi-modal conditional VAE architecture that encodes chemical graphs, LINCS L1000 gene expression signatures, AlphaFold-derived protein structure embeddings, and pharmacokinetic features via modality-specific neural encoders integrated into a joint latent space optimized for bioactivity prediction. The model will be fine-tuned with reinforcement learning using bioactivity as a reward to prioritize molecules with enhanced target potency and drug-like properties, combined with synthetic feasibility filtering and hit triaging to reduce experimental burden.

EXPERIMENT: We will compare the multi-modal model against a chemical-only graph VAE baseline using ChEMBL 29 chemical structures, LINCS gene expression perturbation data, AlphaFold structural data for target proteins, and Open PK pharmacokinetic datasets. Generated candidates will be synthesized or procured, with in vitro bioactivity assessed by enzymatic inhibition IC50 assays; success is defined as a statistically significant >20% reduction in mean IC50 of the top 100 molecules from the multi-modal model (Mann–Whitney U test, p < 0.01), along with higher hit rates below 1 µM, benchmarked against matched random and known active controls.

NOVELTY: Unlike prior generative models focusing primarily on chemical or single-modality data, this work systematically integrates diverse, biologically relevant modalities into a unified generative framework with rigorous multi-task optimization and experimental validation, providing a mechanistically grounded and resource-aware pipeline that advances beyond existing approaches by demonstrating empirical efficacy gains attributable to multi-modal conditioning.

topic: Generative AI for drug discovery and molecular design
text:
IDEA:  
Integrating multi-omics data (genomics, transcriptomics, metabolomics) as biologically informed conditioning vectors into a conditional graph-based variational autoencoder with attention mechanisms will enable generative AI models to design drug candidates with significantly higher target specificity and reduced off-target interactions than models trained solely on chemical structure data.

BACKGROUND:  
Current generative AI methods for drug discovery primarily rely on chemical structure data, limiting their ability to capture complex biological contexts that govern ligand-target specificity. Multi-omics datasets encode disease-relevant molecular states that could guide molecule generation toward more precise target engagement, but their integration into generative frameworks remains underexplored and lacks rigorous validation. Addressing this gap could improve the design of highly selective drug candidates, reducing adverse effects and enhancing therapeutic efficacy.

APPROACH:  
We propose a dual-pipeline framework where a multi-omics-integrated generative model conditions molecule generation on embedded multi-omics signatures from TCGA (genomics and transcriptomics of cancer subtypes) combined with metabolomics profiles from HMDB relevant to target proteins, while a baseline model uses only chemical structure data from ChEMBL 30. Both pipelines employ a conditional graph-based Variational Autoencoder (VGAE) augmented with attention layers to incorporate auxiliary data and are optimized via reinforcement learning with pretrained predictors (Chemprop for molecular properties, DeepAffinity for target binding). Multi-omics embeddings are normalized, weighted, and fused through a biologically motivated scheme ensuring robust and noise-resistant conditioning.

EXPERIMENT:  
We will generate drug candidates for multiple cancer-associated protein targets and quantitatively compare models on predicted binding affinity and off-target binding scores using calibrated molecular docking simulations and validated multi-target binding prediction networks. Statistical significance will be assessed via paired t-tests (p < 0.01), with success defined as ≥10% improvement in mean binding affinity and ≥20% reduction in off-target risk by the multi-omics model versus the chemical-only baseline. Top candidates from both groups will be synthesized and experimentally tested for binding specificity using surface plasmon resonance (SPR) and complementary functional assays against a biologically relevant off-target protein panel.

NOVELTY:  
This work uniquely combines heterogeneous multi-omics datasets into a unified conditioning vector within a graph-based generative architecture enhanced by attention mechanisms, explicitly calibrated and validated against experimental binding data to establish causal links between multi-omics context and drug-target specificity. Unlike prior generative models that focus solely on chemical or structural data or incorporate limited biological context, our approach provides a principled, quantitatively validated multi-omics integration strategy that meaningfully advances the precision of AI-driven molecular design.

topic: Generative AI for drug discovery and molecular design
text:
IDEA: Incorporate differentiable 3D protein-ligand interaction potentials directly into the reverse diffusion sampling of score-based generative models to bias molecule generation toward candidates with improved experimentally validated binding affinity.

BACKGROUND: Developing small molecules with high binding affinity to target proteins remains a central challenge in drug discovery, particularly in effectively leveraging 3D structural interaction information during generative modeling. Existing molecular generative approaches often neglect or approximate protein context, limiting their ability to produce candidates with strong, specific binding. Integrating explicit, physically informed 3D interaction constraints into generative models could substantially enhance the quality of proposed drug candidates.

APPROACH: We extend denoising diffusion probabilistic models (DDPMs) by embedding differentiable scoring functions that encode 3D protein-ligand interaction energies—including hydrogen bonding, hydrophobic contacts, and electrostatics—derived from molecular mechanics force fields or neural approximators such as GNINA. These interaction gradients guide the reverse diffusion process conditioned on the protein binding pocket geometry, effectively biasing molecule generation toward conformations predicted to form stronger binding interactions.
