To maintain chemical diversity and synthetic feasibility, we incorporate ADMET and synthetic accessibility filters with diversity-promoting sampling strategies.

EXPERIMENT: Using the PDBbind v2020 refined set and MOSES 3D dataset with docked conformations from AutoDock Vina for training, we generate candidate molecules for a selected kinase or protease target with well-characterized in vitro binding assays. We compare our Diffusion-3D model against Diffusion-Base (no interaction constraints), REINVENT 4, and GraphAF baselines using metrics including median IC50/Kd improvements on synthesized candidates, statistical significance via Wilcoxon rank-sum tests (p < 0.01), docking score correlations (Pearson r > 0.7), and orthogonal validations such as molecular dynamics-based free energy estimates. Negative (random molecules, known inactives) and positive (known binders/decoys) controls will calibrate assay robustness.

NOVELTY: Unlike prior structure-conditioned generative models that use static or implicit protein information, our method uniquely integrates differentiable, physics-inspired 3D interaction potentials directly into the diffusion sampling gradients, enabling end-to-end biased molecule generation with rigorous theoretical justification. This approach balances constraint-driven targeting with chemical exploration, validated by both computational and experimental data, providing a principled framework to improve binding affinity predictions beyond docking score heuristics.

topic: Generative AI for drug discovery and molecular design
text:
IDEA:  
Incorporating multi-modal biochemical data—specifically gene expression and metabolomics profiles—into a hybrid Transformer-VAE generative model significantly enhances the novelty and in vitro efficacy (lower IC50 values) of designed drug candidates for a defined target compared to models trained solely on chemical structures.

BACKGROUND:  
De novo drug design via generative AI often relies exclusively on chemical structure and bioactivity data, limiting the biological context and potentially missing critical disease-relevant molecular cues. Integrating multi-omics data (transcriptomics and metabolomics) linked to the target’s cellular state offers a promising avenue to generate molecules better tailored to target-specific biochemical environments. However, rigorous experimental validation demonstrating that such multi-modal conditioning improves molecule novelty and functional efficacy remains an open challenge.

APPROACH:  
We propose a joint generative modeling framework based on a hybrid Transformer-VAE architecture that conditions molecule generation on latent embeddings derived from curated, batch-corrected multi-omics datasets—including LINCS L1000 gene expression and Metabolomics Workbench profiles—matched to ChEMBL 30 chemical structures and bioactivities for a well-characterized target (e.g., BRAF kinase). Multi-modal embeddings are encoded via separate graph neural networks and variational encoders and integrated into the molecule latent space, with reinforcement learning optimizing for predicted binding affinity and drug-likeness.

EXPERIMENT:  
We will compare two models: (1) a baseline trained exclusively on chemical structures and (2) a multi-modal conditioned model incorporating gene expression and metabolomics data. Both models will generate candidate molecules which will be assessed computationally for novelty (Tanimoto similarity distributions) and predicted affinity (docking and ML predictors), followed by synthesis and in vitro IC50 measurement against the target. Statistical power analysis will determine the number of compounds tested per model, with negative controls using permuted omics data and benchmarking against state-of-the-art generative frameworks. Success requires the multi-modal model’s candidates to show ≥20% lower median IC50 (p < 0.05 Mann-Whitney U test) and ≥15% higher novelty than baseline.

NOVELTY:  
Unlike prior work focusing solely on chemical structures or incorporating limited biological context, this study rigorously integrates multi-omics latent embeddings from multiple biochemical modalities into a unified generative framework with explicit biological conditioning. The approach is distinguished by its comprehensive data alignment, formal statistical validation including negative controls, and direct experimental demonstration that multi-modal data integration confers measurable advantages in molecular novelty and functional efficacy in vitro.

topic: Mechanistic interpretability of transformer models
text:
IDEA: Incorporating sparsity- and modularity-promoting auxiliary losses during transformer training leads to significantly more mechanistically interpretable, modular attention circuits compared to standard language modeling objectives.

BACKGROUND: While mechanistic interpretability of transformers seeks to reverse-engineer their internal circuits, current models trained solely on next-token prediction often produce entangled, overlapping attention patterns that hinder modular circuit discovery. Explicitly encouraging structural modularity during training remains an open challenge, with unclear effects on interpretability and model performance.

APPROACH: We propose augmenting the standard language modeling loss with carefully designed regularizers that promote modular circuit formation by enforcing sparsity across cross-head attention maps and orthogonality constraints on intermediate representations, inspired by graph clustering and disentangled representation learning. These auxiliary losses aim to induce functionally isolated, interpretable subnetworks within attention heads, facilitating clearer circuit boundaries without degrading perplexity.

EXPERIMENT: We will train GPT-2 small transformer models on OpenWebText2 with and without the proposed auxiliary losses, then evaluate mechanistic interpretability on both OpenWebText2 and WikiText-103 datasets using the Circuit Purity Score (CPS) as the primary metric, supported by neuron-level linguistic probing and expert-verified qualitative circuit visualizations. A minimum 20% CPS improvement over baseline, with perplexity no worse than 5% above baseline, will validate the hypothesis; failure to improve or a CPS drop greater than 5% will falsify it. Multiple random seeds and controlled checkpoints will ensure statistical robustness.

NOVELTY: Unlike prior work focused on post hoc circuit discovery or disentangled representations broadly, this study explicitly integrates modularity-inducing objectives tailored to transformer attention patterns during training, linking structural constraints directly to interpretable mechanistic circuits. This approach bridges theoretical modularity principles with practical training modifications, enabling empirical validation of modularity as a pathway to enhanced transformer interpretability.

topic: Mechanistic interpretability of transformer models
text:
IDEA:  
Investigate the mechanistic modularity and functional dependencies of transformer attention heads by causally intervening on their activations across diverse linguistic tasks, to rigorously quantify whether attention heads form independently ablatable mechanistic subcircuits or exhibit distributed, context-dependent roles.

BACKGROUND:  
While prior mechanistic interpretability work suggests that individual transformer attention heads contribute to specific linguistic phenomena, the extent to which these heads correspond to modular, independently functioning subcircuits remains unclear. Existing analyses often rely on correlation or partial interventions without systematically probing inter-head dependencies or cross-task generalization, leaving open whether mechanistic functions are localized or distributed and context-dependent across linguistic competencies.

APPROACH:  
We combine multiple complementary attribution methods—including Integrated Gradients, Attention Rollout, and perturbation-based causal attribution—with targeted activation patching and ablation of individual and grouped attention heads in pretrained GPT-2 medium. Ablations will be carefully controlled with noise replacement and scaled activation baselines to isolate meaningful mechanistic components. We further theoretically motivate and empirically validate the choice of attention heads as mechanistic units while situating these within broader circuit contexts.

EXPERIMENT:  
We evaluate ablation impacts on three linguistically diverse benchmarks—SyntaxGym for syntactic phenomena, LAMBADA for broad-context semantic prediction, and SuperGLUE’s diagnostic subset for natural language understanding—measuring task-specific performance drops (accuracy, perplexity, syntactic agreement) to assess modularity. Statistical rigor is ensured via multiple runs and significance testing, comparing single-head, subcircuit, and random-head ablations against unablated baselines to detect non-additive and distributed effects.

NOVELTY:  
This work uniquely integrates robust causal intervention frameworks and rigorous statistical analyses to disentangle modularity from distributed mechanistic function in transformer attention heads across multiple, theoretically justified linguistic tasks, going beyond prior interpretability studies that typically analyze isolated behaviors or lack systematic cross-task validation and intervention controls.

topic: Mechanistic interpretability of transformer models
text:
IDEA:  
Transformer models trained on multilingual data develop distinct, language-specific mechanistic circuits for syntactic tasks rather than unified, language-agnostic circuits; this can be causally tested and potentially falsified via rigorously controlled cross-lingual activation patching combined with robust circuit alignment methods.

BACKGROUND:  
While transformer-based multilingual models like mBERT and XLM-R achieve strong cross-lingual performance, it remains an open question whether their internal mechanistic computations are shared across languages or segregated into language-specific circuits. Existing work on mechanistic interpretability has largely focused on monolingual models or single-language circuits, lacking direct causal evidence about multilingual circuit structure. Understanding whether models rely on unified or distinct mechanistic circuits is critical for interpretability, transferability, and robustness of multilingual NLP systems.

APPROACH:  
We propose to identify mechanistic circuits responsible for a universal syntactic phenomenon—subject-verb agreement—across multiple languages (English, German, Spanish, Chinese) using parallel Universal Dependencies treebanks. After finely aligning candidate circuit components across languages via representational similarity analysis and probing consistency, we perform cross-lingual activation patching to causally test whether swapping activations between languages disrupts prediction accuracy. We include rigorous within-language patching and random-component patching controls to isolate language-specific circuit effects. Fine-tuning is minimized or carefully controlled to avoid language-specific adaptation artifacts.

EXPERIMENT:  
Using mBERT or XLM-R fine-tuned or probed on English-EWT, German-GSD, Spanish-GSD, and Chinese-GSD datasets, we measure the relative accuracy change \(\Delta\) in subject-verb agreement predictions when patching activations from one language into another. Baselines include monolingual English BERT within-language patching and random patching controls. Significant negative \(\Delta\) (>10%) for cross-lingual patching implies distinct circuits, whereas negligible \(\Delta\) (<1-2%) falsifies the hypothesis, indicating shared circuits.

NOVELTY:  
This work introduces a novel, causally grounded framework combining mechanistic interpretability tools—activation patching and representational alignment—in a multilingual context with carefully controlled cross-lingual comparisons. Unlike prior studies that either focus on single languages or representational similarity alone, our approach directly tests mechanistic circuit modularity versus unification across languages with rigorous falsifiability criteria and parallel, syntactically matched datasets.

topic: Mechanistic interpretability of transformer models
text:
IDEA:  
Investigate whether mechanistic interpretability and modular functional specialization emerge predominantly at the scale of individual attention heads only in transformer models trained on explicitly modular synthetic tasks, and assess how this phenomenon generalizes across a spectrum of datasets with varying degrees of modularity and complexity using refined multi-scale interpretability metrics.

BACKGROUND:  
Understanding how transformer models internally organize computations is a central challenge in mechanistic interpretability, with prior work suggesting that individual attention heads can specialize in interpretable algorithmic subroutines primarily in synthetic settings with clear modular structure. However, it remains unclear whether such modular specialization arises in models trained on natural language tasks characterized by entangled, hierarchical linguistic phenomena, or if mechanistic modularity should instead be sought at broader architectural scales. Resolving this uncertainty is critical for developing faithful, generalizable interpretability frameworks.

APPROACH:  
We propose a comparative, multi-scale mechanistic interpretability study that trains identical GPT-2 small transformers on a graded suite of datasets spanning from the algorithmically modular Dyck language, through intermediate synthetic languages with partial modularity, to large-scale natural language corpora like OpenWebText and WikiText-103. We will apply refined causal mediation analyses and activation patching not only on individual attention heads but also on MLP layers and cross-layer subnetworks, while developing new functional role metrics grounded in causal interventions and validated probes that move beyond noisy syntactic proxies. This design enables quantification of modular specialization and mechanistic interpretability as a function of dataset modularity and architectural scale.

EXPERIMENT:  
We will evaluate mechanistic specialization by measuring (1) the fraction of attention heads, MLPs, and multi-unit modules that attain ≥70% fidelity in recovering known or proxy subroutines via causal mediation and activation patching, and (2) a modularity index quantifying functional independence through mutual information between module activations and sub-computation outputs. Success is defined as ≥50% of modules achieving these thresholds in modular datasets (e.g., Dyck), with a graded decline expected in less modular natural language datasets (OpenWebText, WikiText-103). Falsification occurs if natural language-trained models achieve comparable modularity and interpretability at any scale, disproving the hypothesis that modular specialization is exclusive to explicitly structured tasks.

NOVELTY:  
Unlike prior work that focuses narrowly on attention heads or single synthetic datasets, this study systematically spans multiple datasets with varying modularity and rigorously expands the mechanistic unit of analysis beyond heads to include broader architectural modules. Additionally, it develops and validates new causal, mechanistically grounded metrics for functional role fidelity in natural language models, providing a more faithful and generalizable framework for assessing modularity and interpretability across realistic transformer training regimes.

topic: Mechanistic interpretability of transformer models
text:
IDEA:  
Specific attention heads in mid-to-late layers of transformer language models instantiate discrete, modular algorithmic subroutines that can be causally isolated and recombined to replicate compositional reasoning tasks, with hypothesis falsified if systematic ablation and recomposition fail to preserve task performance.

BACKGROUND:  
Mechanistic interpretability aims to reverse-engineer how transformers internally implement complex behaviors, yet it remains unclear at what granularity algorithmic computations are localized and whether transformer components like attention heads correspond to modular subroutines. Existing work largely assumes distributed representations, leaving open the question of whether discrete attention heads encode isolatable subroutines for compositional generalization. Establishing such modularity would significantly advance mechanistic understanding and practical interpretability of language models.

APPROACH:  
We will use causal mediation analyses and activation patching to identify attention heads in mid-to-late layers of pre-trained GPT-2 Medium and GPT-3 Ada that have a causal impact on compositional linguistic tasks (SCAN and CFQ). Subsequent experiments will ablate these heads individually and combinatorially, as well as ablate other architectural components (MLPs, layer norm, and full blocks) to disentangle contribution and redundancy. Finally, identified heads will be transplanted into a minimalist Transformer variant, freezing their weights and fine-tuning remaining parameters under controlled retraining protocols to evaluate whether recomposition recovers the original model’s compositional accuracy.

EXPERIMENT:  
Evaluation will focus on compositional generalization splits of SCAN and CFQ, measuring task accuracy under (a) intact model, (b) targeted head ablation, (c) random head ablation, (d) combinatorial ablations including MLPs and blocks, and (e) recomposition of identified heads versus random recombinations. Success requires ablations to cause ≥15 percentage point accuracy drops and recomposition to recover ≥90% of baseline accuracy; failure modes include negligible ablation effects (<5 points drop) or recomposition recovery ≤50%, falsifying modular subroutine hypotheses.

NOVELTY:  
This work rigorously grounds the mechanistic interpretability hypothesis in explicit granularity and modularity assumptions about attention heads, integrating broader architectural ablations and realistic, controlled retraining during recomposition—advancing beyond prior studies by providing formal causal tests of subroutine modularity and transplantability within large-scale transformer models on compositional linguistic benchmarks.

topic: Foundation models for genomics and single-cell biology
text:
IDEA:  
Foundation models pretrained on integrated genomic DNA sequences and matched single-cell transcriptomic data improve prediction of cell-type-specific regulatory element activity beyond models trained on either modality alone.

BACKGROUND:  
Accurate identification of cell-type-specific regulatory elements is critical for understanding gene regulation and cellular function but remains challenging due to the complex interplay between DNA sequence and transcriptional states. While genomic sequence models (e.g., DeepSEA) capture cis-regulatory motifs and single-cell transcriptomic models (e.g., scBERT) capture gene expression heterogeneity, it is unclear if combining these complementary data types in a unified foundation model yields superior predictive power for regulatory activity at cellular resolution. Establishing robust multimodal models would address this critical gap in linking regulatory sequences to their functional impact across diverse cell types.

APPROACH:  
We propose to develop a transformer-based foundation model architecture that encodes nucleotide-level genomic sequences annotated with regulatory element regions alongside cell-type-aggregated single-cell RNA-seq embeddings derived from matched tissues. By employing modality-specific masked token prediction and contrastive learning objectives during joint pretraining, and enabling cross-attention layers for multimodal interaction, the model learns an integrated latent representation capturing both sequence and expression context. Three models will be trained separately on (1) genomic sequence data only, (2) single-cell transcriptomic data only, and (3) combined multimodal inputs, using rigorous batch correction and cell-type matching informed by paired multi-omic datasets to ensure alignment.

EXPERIMENT:  
We will evaluate predictive performance on a held-out benchmark comprising experimentally validated, cell-type-resolved regulatory elements from the ENCODE Phase 3 and DeepSEA challenge test sets, filtered for peripheral blood mononuclear cells and additional tissues with paired chromatin accessibility and single-cell RNA-seq data from the Human Cell Atlas. Metrics will include area under the precision-recall curve (AUPRC) and area under the receiver operating characteristic curve (AUROC), supplemented by cell-type specificity scores derived from perturbation-based single-cell multi-omic benchmarks. Success is defined as the multimodal model outperforming the best single-modality baseline by at least 5% absolute AUPRC improvement, with statistical significance assessed by cross-validation and permutation testing. Ablation and modality-shuffling controls will confirm genuine multimodal complementarity.

NOVELTY:  
This work uniquely integrates high-resolution genomic and single-cell transcriptomic data into a unified foundation model with cross-modal attention, surpassing prior single-modality approaches such as DeepSEA and scBERT. It rigorously addresses cell-type matching and batch effects using multi-omic references, introduces tailored contrastive and masked-language objectives for multimodal pretraining, and benchmarks on robust, cell-type-specific regulatory element sets including perturbation-based validation, thereby advancing both the methodology and biological interpretability of foundation models in regulatory genomics.

topic: Foundation models for genomics and single-cell biology
text:
IDEA: Foundation models pre-trained on integrated multi-omics single-cell data (scRNA-seq and scATAC-seq) can predict cell-type-specific regulatory elements with significantly higher accuracy than models trained on single-modality data alone.

BACKGROUND: Accurately identifying regulatory elements such as enhancers and promoters at single-cell resolution remains a critical challenge due to the noisy and incomplete nature of single-modality data and limitations of bulk-derived annotations. Existing models typically leverage either transcriptomics or chromatin accessibility data independently, missing the complementary regulatory information that multi-omics integration could provide. Establishing whether foundation models that jointly embed multi-modal single-cell data offer a tangible predictive advantage for regulatory element discovery is an open problem with broad implications for genomics and cell biology.

APPROACH: We will develop and pre-train transformer-based foundation models on paired single-cell multi-omics data, specifically integrating scRNA-seq and scATAC-seq modalities within a joint embedding framework using masked token prediction and contrastive learning objectives. These models will be compared against single-modality baselines—state-of-the-art deep convolutional models (e.g., SCALE, PeakVI) for scATAC-seq and transformer models (e.g., scBERT) for scRNA-seq—using harmonized architectures and training protocols. Fine-tuning will target supervised classification of candidate regulatory elements in a cell-type-specific manner, leveraging linked genomic sequences and expression profiles.

EXPERIMENT: We will evaluate performance on publicly available multi-omics datasets, including 10x Genomics Multiome PBMC data and multi-tissue Human Cell Atlas datasets, using rigorously curated cell-type-specific regulatory element annotations derived from ENCODE and SCREEN databases intersected with chromatin accessibility peaks. Model accuracy will be quantified by precision-recall AUC (PR-AUC) and ROC-AUC averaged over at least 10 distinct cell types, with success defined as ≥5% absolute improvement in PR-AUC of the multi-modal model over the best single-modality baseline. Calibration metrics and biological enrichment analyses near relevant marker genes will further validate predictions. Failure to exceed single-modality model performance by this margin will falsify the hypothesis.

NOVELTY: Unlike prior work that often uses single modalities or bulk annotations, this study rigorously integrates complementary single-cell chromatin and transcriptomic data within a unified foundation model framework, controls for training and architecture confounders, and employs improved cell-type-resolved ground truth to robustly assess the value of multi-omics pretraining for regulatory element prediction. This approach advances beyond existing bioinformatics methods by combining theoretical justification, strict experimental controls, and comprehensive multi-tissue evaluation to establish the true utility of foundation models in single-cell regulatory genomics.

topic: Foundation models for genomics and single-cell biology
text:
IDEA:  
Develop a transformer-based multimodal foundation model pretrained jointly on genomic and single-cell transcriptomic data to improve cell-type-specific gene regulatory network (GRN) inference, validated by independent single-cell perturbation experiments.

BACKGROUND:  
Predicting accurate cell-type-specific GRNs remains a major challenge due to the complex interplay of genomic regulatory elements and dynamic gene expression programs. Existing GRN inference methods often rely on single data modalities or classical integration approaches that do not fully leverage large-scale multimodal pretraining, limiting their ability to capture causal regulatory relationships at single-cell resolution. A unified foundation model pretrained on combined genomic and transcriptomic data could enhance predictive power and biological interpretability.

APPROACH:  
We propose a transformer architecture that integrates DNA sequence features, epigenomic signals (e.g., ATAC-seq, histone modifications), and single-cell RNA-seq expression profiles through joint self-supervised pretraining combining masked token prediction and contrastive learning to align regulatory elements with cell-type-specific expression. Fine-tuning will be performed on curated, experimentally validated GRN datasets to specialize the model for cell-type-specific regulatory edge prediction.

EXPERIMENT:  
Model performance will be evaluated on independent Perturb-seq single-cell gene perturbation datasets (e.g., Replogle et al. 2020, Dixit et al. 2016) by predicting transcription factor–target gene edges across multiple cell types, benchmarked using PR-AUC and F1-score. Baselines include models pretrained on only genomic or only transcriptomic data, classical GRN inference tools (SCENIC, GRNBoost2), and multi-omics integration without foundation pretraining (MOFA+). Statistical significance will be assessed via bootstrap testing, with success defined as ≥10% absolute PR-AUC improvement over the best baseline.

NOVELTY:  
This work uniquely combines large-scale multimodal foundation model pretraining with rigorous, perturbation-based validation of cell-type-specific GRNs, providing a theoretically grounded framework that explicitly aligns genomic regulatory context with single-cell expression dynamics. Unlike prior multimodal or classical methods, it integrates heterogeneous data modalities at scale with transformer architectures and contrastive learning, enabling improved causal inference of regulatory networks with direct experimental validation.

topic: Foundation models for genomics and single-cell biology
text:
IDEA:  
Foundation models pretrained on harmonized, integrated single-cell multi-omics datasets (scRNA-seq, scATAC-seq, and single-cell DNA methylation) will more accurately predict novel cell-type-specific regulatory elements than models trained on transcriptomics alone, as validated by rigorously controlled CRISPR interference data.

BACKGROUND:  
Identifying functional regulatory elements that control cell identity remains a central challenge in genomics and single-cell biology. While single-cell transcriptomic data provide valuable gene expression profiles, regulatory activity is governed by multiple interconnected layers such as chromatin accessibility and DNA methylation, which are often not fully leveraged in predictive models. Existing models either focus on single modalities or bulk data and lack robust validation against causal perturbation assays like CRISPRi, limiting their ability to generalize to novel regulatory elements across diverse cell types.

APPROACH:  
We will develop a transformer-based foundation model that integrates modality-specific embeddings from single-cell transcriptomic, chromatin accessibility, and DNA methylation data into a shared latent space via a cross-modal attention mechanism. This Multi-Omics FM will be pretrained on harmonized Human Cell Atlas 10x Multiome (scRNA + scATAC) datasets across multiple tissues and the Mouse Brain Atlas single-cell methylome, with batch correction and alignment strategies to mitigate cross-species and cross-tissue heterogeneity. The model will be fine-tuned on cell-type-specific CRISPRi datasets, incorporating negative controls and adjusting for confounders such as guide RNA efficiency and chromatin state, to predict regulatory element impact quantitatively.

EXPERIMENT:  
We will benchmark the Multi-Omics FM against a Transcriptomics-Only FM pretrained on matched scRNA-seq data, classical machine learning models (random forest, gradient boosting) trained on transcriptomics, state-of-the-art bulk multi-omics deep learning models adapted for single-cell inputs (e.g., DeepSEA, Basset), and the scBERT foundation model pretrained exclusively on scRNA-seq. Performance will be evaluated on held-out cell-type-matched CRISPRi-validated regulatory element datasets using area under the precision-recall curve (AUPRC) and AUROC, requiring a statistically significant (p < 0.01 via bootstrapping) ≥10% relative increase in AUPRC by the Multi-Omics FM to support the hypothesis.

NOVELTY:  
Unlike prior work that either focuses on single-modality foundation models or bulk multi-omics models without direct causal validation, our approach uniquely integrates triple-modality single-cell data with advanced cross-modal attention to learn joint regulatory representations. We explicitly validate predictions against rigorously controlled, cell-type-matched CRISPRi perturbation experiments, providing mechanistic insight and demonstrating meaningful improvements in regulatory element prediction accuracy that justify the complexity of multi-omics integration.

topic: Foundation models for genomics and single-cell biology
text:
IDEA:  
Pretraining transformer-based foundation models on integrated multimodal single-cell data (RNA-seq, ATAC-seq, and protein expression) enables more accurate prediction of novel cell states after perturbations than models trained on any single modality alone, as validated by quantitative comparisons on independent experimental perturbation datasets.

BACKGROUND:  
Accurately predicting novel cell states arising from genetic or environmental perturbations is a central challenge in single-cell biology and critical for understanding cellular heterogeneity and disease mechanisms. Existing models typically leverage single-modal data (e.g., RNA or ATAC alone), limiting their ability to capture the complementary regulatory and functional signals inherent to cellular state transitions. Multimodal single-cell datasets offer a richer representation, but it remains unclear whether foundation models pretrained on such data provide substantial predictive gains for unseen perturbations.

APPROACH:  
We will develop a multimodal transformer foundation model that jointly encodes single-cell RNA, chromatin accessibility (ATAC), and surface protein expression by concatenating modality-specific token and modality-type embeddings, trained using masked modality prediction and cross-modal contrastive losses. Three unimodal baseline models of matched architecture and capacity will be separately pretrained on RNA-seq, ATAC-seq, or protein expression alone using analogous objectives. During fine-tuning, all models will predict perturbed cell states from baseline profiles and perturbation metadata, facilitating direct comparison.

EXPERIMENT:  
Pretraining will use integrated multimodal PBMC datasets: the 10x Genomics Multiome (RNA + ATAC, ~10k cells) and the Human Cell Atlas CITE-seq PBMC dataset (RNA + surface proteins). Evaluation will be performed on the independent Kang et al. (2021) multimodal perturbation dataset containing PBMCs subjected to cytokine stimulations and CRISPR knockouts profiled with single-cell multiomics. Prediction accuracy will be quantified by Adjusted Rand Index (ARI) and silhouette scores comparing predicted versus observed cell clusters, and average cosine similarity between predicted and experimental cell embeddings. Success is defined as a ≥10% improvement in ARI and ≥0.05 increase in cosine similarity by the multimodal model relative to the best unimodal baseline.

NOVELTY:  
This study rigorously quantifies the added value of multimodal foundation models over unimodal counterparts for prospective perturbation outcome prediction using controlled, modality-specific baselines and independent perturbation datasets—surpassing prior work that focused primarily on unimodal integration or retrospective analyses. It uniquely combines a theoretically motivated multimodal transformer architecture with cross-modal contrastive and masked prediction objectives, validated through precise, biologically meaningful metrics tied to causal perturbation effects.

topic: Quantum error correction in NISQ devices
text:
IDEA:  
Implementing an adaptive quantum error correction (QEC) framework that dynamically selects and switches between optimized encoding schemes based on real-time qubit noise characterization in NISQ devices will reduce logical error rates by over 50% compared to static QEC codes under identical hardware conditions.

BACKGROUND:  
NISQ devices operate with limited qubit counts and coherence times, making fixed QEC codes suboptimal in the presence of temporally and spatially varying noise. Current static QEC approaches do not leverage real-time noise fluctuations, leaving open the challenge of dynamically adapting error correction to improve logical fidelity within realistic hardware constraints.

APPROACH:  
We propose a low-latency adaptive QEC control system that monitors qubit-specific noise metrics (e.g., T1, T2, and gate error rates) on IBM Quantum Falcon processors and dynamically selects from a precomputed set of QEC codes—including varying-distance surface codes and Bacon-Shor codes—optimized for the instantaneous noise profile by minimizing an estimated logical error cost function. Code switching is performed between rounds of logical circuit executions to minimize overhead and coherence penalties.

EXPERIMENT:  
We will benchmark logical error rates on ibmq_guadalupe using repeated executions of logical circuits (5-qubit repetition code and small logical Clifford circuits) under both static QEC codes (fixed distance-3 surface code) and the adaptive QEC scheme, correlating results with in-situ noise telemetry and syndrome measurements. Logical error rates derived from hardware runs and noise-aware simulations will validate if the adaptive method achieves at least a 50% logical error reduction over the best static code baseline; failure to do so consistently across noise regimes falsifies the hypothesis.

NOVELTY:  
Unlike prior work limited to either static QEC or post-processing error mitigation, this approach integrates real-time noise telemetry with dynamic code switching under realistic latency and hardware constraints, providing a rigorously controlled experimental validation of adaptive QEC benefits in the NISQ regime.

topic: Quantum error correction in NISQ devices
text:
IDEA:  
Implementing real-time, hardware-tailored quantum error correction codes that exploit dominant noise asymmetries on IBM’s Falcon superconducting and IonQ’s trapped-ion NISQ devices will extend logical qubit coherence times by at least 50% compared to generic QEC codes under matched experimental conditions.

BACKGROUND:  
Current NISQ devices suffer from noise dominated by asymmetrical error channels—such as amplitude damping in superconducting qubits and phase-flip errors in trapped ions—that generic QEC codes do not fully leverage. While prior work has demonstrated generic QEC and error mitigation, significant improvements in logical qubit lifetime require noise-aware, hardware-specific QEC strategies that adapt to temporal noise drifts and practical hardware constraints. Addressing these challenges is critical to advancing fault-tolerant quantum computation on near-term platforms.

APPROACH:  
We will perform in situ, real-time noise characterization using IBMQ Casablanca’s 27-qubit calibration datasets and IonQ’s native noise profiles immediately before and during experiments to capture temporal drifts. Using these data, we will design and implement bias-preserving and asymmetric syndrome extraction tailored QEC codes optimized for each device’s dominant error channel, employing hardware-compatible pulse-level control and adaptive decoding within cloud-access constraints. Logical qubit coherence times will be measured under repeated syndrome extraction and real-time decoding, compared against standard surface code and generic 5-qubit code baselines compiled and run under identical device conditions.

EXPERIMENT:  
Logical qubit coherence will be quantified as the duration until logical error rates exceed 1%, measured across a statistically significant number of trials (e.g., ≥1000) with confidence intervals established via bootstrapping. Benchmarking will use IBMQ Casablanca calibration data and IonQ published noise profiles for noise asymmetry identification, comparing tailored QEC performance against generic codes on both platforms. Success is defined by achieving ≥50% extension in logical coherence time over generic QEC codes after accounting for device calibration drift and statistical uncertainty.

NOVELTY:  
This work uniquely integrates continuous, real-time noise tomography with hardware- and noise-aware QEC code design explicitly adapted to cloud-accessible NISQ hardware constraints, including pulse-level implementation and adaptive decoding latency. Unlike prior studies focusing on static noise models or theoretical thresholds, this approach demonstrates practical, demonstrable improvements in logical qubit performance on commercial NISQ platforms by fully exploiting dominant noise asymmetries.

topic: Quantum error correction in NISQ devices
text:
IDEA: Implementing adaptive quantum error correction codes that leverage low-latency, real-time noise characterization to dynamically adjust decoding on NISQ superconducting qubit devices reduces logical error rates by at least 30% compared to static QEC codes under identical hardware calibration conditions.

BACKGROUND: Current quantum error correction (QEC) implementations on NISQ devices typically rely on static error models derived from periodic calibrations, which fail to capture temporal noise fluctuations and non-stationarities inherent to superconducting qubits. This limits achievable logical qubit fidelity and obscures potential gains from noise-adaptive strategies. Demonstrating practical, real-time adaptive QEC on existing hardware with tight coherence-time constraints remains an open challenge critical for bridging toward fault-tolerant quantum computing.

APPROACH: We propose to implement the [[5,1,3]] quantum error correction code on IBM Quantum superconducting processors using Qiskit Runtime to orchestrate rapid noise diagnostics—via streamlined randomized benchmarking tailored for speed—and Bayesian or machine learning-based decoders that update error syndrome interpretation dynamically within each QEC cycle. Real-time noise parameters, collected immediately preceding and during syndrome extraction, feed into the adaptive decoder to optimize thresholding and error correction decisions within the device coherence window.

EXPERIMENT: Logical error rates per QEC cycle will be measured by repeatedly preparing the logical |0⟩ state, performing multiple rounds of syndrome extraction, and measuring logical qubit survival probability on IBM Quantum Falcon or Eagle backends. We will compare adaptive decoding against a static baseline employing fixed decoding rules calibrated offline. Statistical significance of ≥30% logical error rate reduction will be evaluated with paired t-tests over ≥1000 runs while recording decoder latency and resource overhead to validate feasibility.

NOVELTY: Unlike previous studies that rely on offline noise characterization or lack integration of real-time feedback, this work demonstrates an end-to-end adaptive QEC pipeline with rigorous latency benchmarking on real NISQ hardware. It uniquely combines fast, lightweight noise estimation protocols compatible with Qiskit Runtime constraints and dynamic decoding on a well-characterized [[5,1,3]] code, advancing beyond prior adaptive QEC proposals primarily demonstrated in simulation or with static decoders.

topic: Quantum error correction in NISQ devices
text:
IDEA:  
Integrating real-time, closed-loop machine learning feedback with syndrome measurements in NISQ devices can dynamically adapt decoding strategies to reduce logical qubit error rates by over 50% compared to static minimum-weight perfect matching and offline neural decoders under realistic noise models.

BACKGROUND:  
Quantum error correction (QEC) in NISQ devices remains limited by noise correlations, temporal instabilities, and hardware constraints that static decoders fail to address effectively. Existing decoders, including MWPM and pre-trained neural networks, do not leverage real-time feedback during syndrome acquisition, restricting their ability to adapt to evolving error environments and measurement latency, thereby impeding progress toward practical fault-tolerance.

APPROACH:  
We propose a recurrent neural network-based decoder (e.g., LSTM) trained via curriculum learning to operate in a true closed-loop manner, continually updating its decoding policy as syndrome data streams in real time. This ML decoder will incorporate feedback to adjust syndrome measurement scheduling and error mitigation dynamically, explicitly modeling temporal and cross-error correlations. Rigorous latency models and noise simulations calibrated to IBM Surface-17 and Google Sycamore datasets ensure realistic implementation constraints are respected.

EXPERIMENT:  
We will benchmark logical error rates using ≥10^5 Monte Carlo runs on both IBM Quantum Experience’s Surface-17 experimental syndrome datasets and synthetically generated data from Qiskit Aer noise models tuned to Google's Sycamore parameters. The ML decoder’s performance will be compared against (1) offline MWPM decoding and (2) a static, pretrained neural network decoder without feedback adaptation. Success is defined as a consistent >50% relative reduction in logical error rate over MWPM across all datasets and noise scenarios, with failure to exceed 30% reduction falsifying the hypothesis.

NOVELTY:  
Unlike prior ML or adaptive decoders that operate offline or lack integrated feedback loops, our method uniquely combines real-time recurrent learning with closed-loop control under realistic hardware latency and noise conditions, establishing theoretical bounds on when dynamic feedback decoding outperforms static schemes. This approach advances practical QEC by explicitly addressing temporal noise correlations, feedback latency, and adaptive measurement scheduling—key bottlenecks unaddressed in existing architectures.

topic: Quantum error correction in NISQ devices
text:
IDEA: Implementing adaptive, real-time feedback quantum error correction protocols on superconducting NISQ devices will reduce logical qubit error rates by more than 30% compared to static QEC schemes under matched noise conditions.

BACKGROUND: Current NISQ devices suffer from relatively high error rates that limit practical quantum computation, and while static quantum error correction (QEC) codes have been demonstrated, their performance is constrained by limited coherence times and feedback latency. A key open challenge is whether real-time, low-latency adaptive feedback within QEC cycles can provide a significant, practical improvement in logical error rates on near-term hardware despite these constraints.

APPROACH: We propose to implement adaptive QEC protocols using [[4,2,2]] and [[5,1,3]] quantum codes where syndrome measurements trigger mid-circuit, real-time corrections conditioned on outcomes, enabled by FPGA-based low-latency classical controllers integrated with IBM’s 27-qubit Falcon processors. The protocol involves rigorous noise characterization and measurement error mitigation, combined with fast classical signal processing to ensure feedback occurs well within qubit coherence times to maximize error suppression.

EXPERIMENT: We will benchmark logical error rates on Quantum Volume 8 and 16 circuits and OpenQASM 2.0 benchmark circuits (Bernstein-Vazirani and Grover’s search) under three conditions: (a) no QEC, (b) static QEC without feedback, and (c) adaptive real-time feedback QEC. Logical error probabilities will be estimated from ≥1000 runs per circuit, using bootstrapped confidence intervals and noise stability monitoring. A >30% logical error rate reduction of adaptive QEC over static QEC will confirm the hypothesis; less than 15% improvement will falsify it.

NOVELTY: This work explicitly addresses and quantifies real-time feedback latency relative to hardware coherence constraints using FPGA-integrated controllers, incorporates stringent noise and measurement error mitigation protocols, and provides theoretical and numerical support predicting adaptive QEC gains on realistic NISQ noise models—advancing beyond prior static QEC demonstrations and theoretical proposals lacking practical, hardware-integrated adaptive feedback validation.
